2.text: As an instance of the contrary, an extract from a description of a

3.text: Chukchee funeral, taken down from the mouth of a native, may be cited.

4.text: “Then they lay down rollers under the sledge and try to draw it. (They ask the deceased)

5.text: ‘Of all those present here, say straightly whether anything ill shall befall them. Tell that about all,

6.text: one by one, not hiding anything.’ If, on asking about some particular person, the sledge runs

7.text: smoothly and without hitch, he will surely die.”¹

8.text: The method of divination by suspension is widely spread among both

9.text: the Reindeer and the Maritime Chukchee, and is employed in almost all cases

10.text: of life. Once, while in a camp on the Wolverene River the night before a

11.text: great race, I was weighing some medicine on a small brass balance. A man

12.text: who sat close by wanted to have a look at the balance, and when he took

13.text: it from my hand, of course it began swinging. The Chukchee took this as

14.text: a sign that the balance wanted to be used for soothsaying. He took advantage

15.text: of this to ask it about the arrangement of the race for the morrow.

16.text: “Shall we arrange it together, or separately?” asked he. “Give a good

17.text: sign! Give a favorable omen!” There were two men desiring to arrange

18.text: the race, and it was a question whether they should join their stakes, or not.

19.text: The balance gave an answer in the required sense. The man asked several

20.text: other questions, which were all answered favorably, because the unstable thing

21.text: swayed to and fro with the slightest motion of the hand of the performer.

22.text: Suddenly, when he put forward a question about the foot-race, the balance

23.text: stood still. One of the cords supporting the plates became hooked to the

24.text: end of the lever, and its free motion was disturbed. “Desist, desist!” cried

25.text: the other people, frightened; but it was too late. Now, when the balance

26.text: did give an unfavorable answer, it was necessary to coax it to change it, and

27.text: to answer more acceptably in its new, entangled position. The experiment

28.text: took over half an hour, and still the balance would not answer satisfactorily.

29.text: Divination with suspended objects is well known also among the Asiatic

30.text: Eskimo and among the Koryak. Those on the Pacific side use their amulets,

31.text: known by the name of “grandmother” (aˊn˙ai), for this purpose. In a Koryak

32.text: tale, a spirit-woman makes her husband use for this purpose his own penis.

33.text: By its motion they are able to determine the movements of human people,

34.text: who flee before their approach. Many Chukchee tales also mention the custom

35.text: of keˊlet trying to foretell the success of their man-hunting by swinging a

36.text: human skull. This serves them as a divining-stone equally as well as the skull

37.text: of an animal serves man for the same purpose.

38.text: Among the Kamchadal, according to Steller,² a woman shaman used to

39.text: sit in a corner, and, winding a red thread around one of her legs, try to

40.text: lift it from the ground. If the leg seemed heavy to lift, a negative answer
